item.title: A.I. Bubble Talk Enters the Conversation at DealBook Summit
item.description:
As tech stocks wavered Wednesday morning, conversation at the DealBook Summit turned to bubbles and sky-high valuations for artificial intelligence companies aspiring to go public.

As for the bubble question, opinion differs.

Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, told Andrew Ross Sorkin in a morning session that she believed there was a “very ambitious price valuation which stands to be corrected eventually.” On the flip side, Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, one of the world’s leading A.I. companies, said there might be “ups and downs of valuations here or there,” but the overall “trend is going to be strong.”

Their comments at the annual summit get at a debate dominating discussion on Wall Street and Silicon Valley, especially with Anthropic expected to price its initial public offering, a possible record-breaker, later on Wednesday. The question on investors’ minds: How fast and how much longer can the A.I. industry keep growing?

Broadly across the industry, investors have become increasingly wary of runaway spending and increasingly lofty valuations of A.I. companies. The Nasdaq Composite index, a benchmark for tech stocks, has tumbled from its October high, underscoring those jitters. In the past month, the beatings have been, in part, driven by the departure of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, as well as fears of a slowdown in data center build out after Democrats took control of Congress in the midterm elections.

item.title: OpenAI Executives Say They Have to Strike a Balance Between Safety and Progress
item.description:
OpenAI’s chief executive said Wednesday that pushing the safe advancement of artificial intelligence comes with inherent trade-offs, and the company had to strike a balance between prioritizing safety while continuing progress on developing A.I.

“We’re not going to be able to make everybody happy,” Sam Altman said at the DealBook Summit

If OpenAI only focuses on being “max pedal to the metal,” he added, “People will say, ‘Well, you know, please don’t kill us all.’”

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, has been under heightened scrutiny in recent months after its A.I. agents went rogue and hacked companies, including the open-source A.I. platform Hugging Face, and government systems.

Those were learning experiences, Mr. Altman said. OpenAI follows “iterative deployment,” he added, and the “only way that we have known how to make this technology safe is to confront reality,” suggesting that the risks couldn’t be known without having been tested in the real world.

OpenAI, along with other A.I. companies, has signed a voluntary agreement to conduct risk reviews and work with third-party evaluators. The company said on Monday that it was embedding independent safety researchers from third-party groups, including METR and Apollo Research, to evaluate OpenAI’s models against various safety measures.

“The models are now capable enough that we need to think about safety, security, alignment — that’s new. And that’s actually been a huge cultural shift,” said Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president and co-founder. “It’s not any one company. It’s really a whole industrywide shift.”

With its rival Anthropic on the verge of a public offering, Altman said OpenAI was still advancing toward its own I.P.O. “We plan to be a public company at some point,” Mr. Altman said.

Mr. Brockman has an equity stake worth at least $30 billion in OpenAI, but Mr. Altman famously owns no shares in the giant start-up. “When we were first setting up the structure, I said to him, ‘You should take equity,’” Mr. Brockman said, referring to the C.E.O.

“I should have listened to Greg,” Mr. Altman said, eliciting laughter. But he said that not having equity had not affected his work at OpenAI. “I don’t think you could argue that I have not acted with full commitment to the company.”

Mr. Brockman drew a contrast between his company’s structure and that of Anthropic, where the seven co-founders hold 50.1 percent of total voting control. “We’re the only company where the founders don’t have super majority control,” he said.

Mr. Altman has previously said the company is delaying its I.P.O. plans till next year to focus on safety issues. Earlier this month, OpenAI raised $11 billion as part of a fund-raising round valued at $1.25 trillion. That’s lower than the $30 billion it initially sought to raise at a valuation as high as $1.5 trillion.

Anthropic is expected to list its shares publicly on Thursday in what could be the world’s largest I.P.O. Earlier this month, Anthropic set a price range of $70 to $78 per share, which would value the company at $1.26 trillion to $1.41 trillion.

item.title: Mark Carney Says Canada Will Not Back Down in Trade Talks With U.S.
item.description:
Canada’s relationship with the Trump administration continues to look frosty. But its efforts to bolster ties with China are showing promise.

Appearing remotely from Shenzhen, China, after long day of meetings, including a session with President Trump, Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada said at the DealBook Summit on Wednesday that Canada would not back down in its trade battle with the United States.

On the other hand, he said talks with China were “going exceptionally well.”

“We reached an agreement, we reduced tariffs in over 90 percent of trade irritants,” he said. “And of course, I’m speaking about our trade negotiations with China. They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”

He added: “Now, if you’re asking about the United States, well, we continue to have a series of issues there.”

Mr. Carney is wrapping up an eight-day tour, which has taken him from Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia and finally China for the APEC summit. All of it in the cause of diversifying Canada’s economy away from its heavy dependence on the United States.

Asked if he now trusts Xi Jinping, China’s leader, more than Mr. Trump, Mr. Carney offered an indirect reply. “We look for situations where there is alignment, and we trust alignment,” he said.

Mr. Carney emphasized, as he has in the past, that Canada’s expanded relationship with China would have careful guardrails. And he dismissed the idea that Canada’s growing relationship with China would leave Canada trading one dependence for another, saying, for example, that he did not think selling canola, an oil seed, to China would be “compromising our sovereignty.”

Before a leaders’ dinner Wednesday evening in China, Mr. Carney had an unscheduled meeting with Mr. Trump. It did not advance Canada’s cause in the trade talks, the prime minister said.

“We had a very nice discussion this evening, so I’ll hang on to that,” Mr. Carney said. “Look, has it changed? I would say no is the short answer.”

Any resolution of the trade war, which had place tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian auto, steel and aluminum exports, will take a major change in policy in Washington, Mr. Carney said. The prime minister also rejected Mr. Trump’s repeated assertions that Canada had no leverage in negotiations with Washington.

“Our cards is that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said.

item.title: David Ellison Confirms Elon Musk Invested in Skydance
item.description:
David Ellison, the chief executive of Skydance, confirmed at the DealBook Summit on Wednesday that Elon Musk had invested in his media goliath, which was born out of a $110 billion deal combining Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery earlier this year.

“He doesn’t invest in a lot of companies,” Mr. Ellison said of Mr. Musk. “So to have his vote of confidence, and to have him as a shareholder, is an honor and a privilege.”

Skydance closed its acquisition last month, aided by a personal financial guarantee by David Ellison’s father, Larry. In addition to Mr. Musk, several other investors helped to contribute equity to the deal, lightening Larry Ellison’s personal load. Three sovereign wealth funds committed $24 billion and Laurene Powell Jobs invested $250 million.

Still, Mr. Musk’s investment, reported to be around $1 billion, brought attention in part because of Mr. Musk’s growing media influence as the owner of the social media platform X. Mr. Musk leads Tesla and SpaceX, which operates Starlink, the internet satellite service. There has been speculation that Starlink might offer Paramount content on its service, which is used by a number of airlines.

Mr. Ellison left the door open to future collaboration with the tech mogul. It would be “a privilege,” he said, “if there was any opportunity to be able to collaborate with him in the future.” Still, he added, “there’s nothing that we can comment on.”

Mr. Ellison also spoke about his father, who is the founder of Oracle. Larry Ellison is friends with Mr. Musk and is a past investor in his companies, having committed about $1 billion to Mr. Musk’s deal to buy Twitter.

David Ellison said he was raised by “a single mother” after his parents’ divorce when he was 3 years old. As a youth, Mr. Ellison said, “We saw each other, you know, once a year, every other year.” That later changed: “Couldn’t be closer now.”

Mr. Ellison spoke a little about the company’s long road to close its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, including the regulatory review, which caught Hollywood’s attention when President Trump implied at one point he would involve himself in the process. “When it comes to the D.O.J., we went through the front door,” Mr. Ellison said of the Department of Justice, seemingly eschewing the idea his company had sought a political workaround in securing approval of the deal.

In discussing what the company would look like going forward, Mr. Ellison also addressed what CBS and CNN might look like, now that they share the same corporate parent.

“There might be some news sharing in the future,” Mr. Ellison said. “But right now, we’re happy operating them as they are.”

Mr. Ellison also emphasized that the news organizations — CNN is run by Mark Thompson while Bari Weiss leads CBS News — would remain editorially independent.

item.title: Nvidia’s Interim C.E.O. Tries to Soothe a Rattled Company: ‘We’ve Got This.’
item.description:
Shortly after 9 a.m. local time on Wednesday, Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive, took the stage inside the company’s headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif., and tried to exude calm.

It had been barely six days since she assumed the top job of the wildly profitable chip maker that has been rocked by revelations that its charismatic and visionary co-founder had two affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence services determined was feeding information to Beijing. The all-hands meeting that Ms. Kress and other executives had convened, a livestream of which was reviewed by The New York Times, was an attempt to soothe the anxieties of a rattled company.

“Our ambition will not change,” Ms. Kress said, who sounded calm and confident as she sat perched on a stool. “Our passion to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners and shareholders will not change.”

She added: “Just remember, we’ve got this.”

In a the span of a month, Nvidia employees have learned that Mr. Huang had multiple affairs and had misled the board about behavior that was at odds with the company’s “code of conduct, standards and cultural norms.”

Mr. Huang resigned in the wake of those revelations, shocking people from Silicon Valley to Washington to Beijing, many of whom had come to see him as the figurehead of the A.I. boom. Nvidia’s market value, which was within a whisper of $6 trillion a month ago, has plummeted to $3.66 trillion.

Last week, Nvidia’s board named Ms. Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as its interim chief executive. It has hired a search firm to find a permanent leader. It also is moving forward with an independent investigation, led by Wachtell Lipton, an outside law firm, into Mr. Huang’s behavior.

Mr. Huang and his allies have mounted a campaign over the past week to return him to the top of the company he started more than three decades ago at a Denny’s in Silicon Valley.

In a call with Wall Street analysts on Tuesday, Harvey C. Jones, the chair of the company’s board, made clear that Mr. Huang would not return.

The back and forth has left employees confused. Some have rallied behind Mr. Huang, signing letters and writing social media posts in support of his return.

“Jensen touched every single employee on an emotional level, genuinely cared about every single developer, and cherished every fragile research idea,” Nik Spirin, an A.I. engineer at Nvidia, wrote in a social media post. “He was both the soul and the mind of the company and the ecosystem.”

Others are looking forward to a future without him. Over the past year, Mr. Huang has alienated parts of this work force by allying himself with President Trump and undermining a plan by other tech companies to develop a systematic way to evaluate the safety of A.I. systems before their release, said three current and former employees who were not authorized to speak publicly about internal company matters.

Wednesday’s meeting began with video footage of company leaders making speeches and demonstrating products. The audio over that video included words that seemed relevant to the moment:

“Nvidia has a history of persevering.”

“It’s all about tenacity as a company.”

“This is the most incredible company on the planet.”

Ms. Kress then took the stage with the executive team and read written remarks. She praised the team behind her, saying “I know this team. I know how much they care for the company and the work.”

Ahead of Nvidia’s all-company meetings, the leadership team solicits questions from employees. The questions on Wednesday largely focused on Mr. Huang’s resignation.

Mr. Jones joined Ms. Kress onstage and shared details of his own Nvidia journey. He joined the board in 2004. He spoke about how his personal relationship with Mr. Huang had made the chain of events over the past week difficult for the board.

“The board was and is fully aware of Jensen’s monumental contribution to the company,” Mr. Jones said. “Several of the board, including me, worked with him for many years and counted him as a friend.”

Mr. Jones reiterated what he told Wall Street analysts on Tuesday.

“It is unrealistic to think we can find a Jensen clone,” Mr. Jones said. “He was one of a kind. That said, there are dynamic leaders out there with demonstrated intellect, high tech engineering experience, strategic thinking, cultural compatibility and a track record of success.”

Chris Malachowsky, a Nvidia co-founder, choked up as he spoke about the situation the company has found itself in and thanked the board for its leadership. Then, he recounted how in the company’s early days, he, Mr. Huang and fellow co-founder Curtis Priem spent much of their time talking about the culture they wanted to instill in Nvidia.

They had a series of core values, he said. Maintain the highest standards in everything they do. Be intellectually honest. Innovate in everything they do. Be direct and candid in communications.

“Those have stood the test of time,” Mr. Malachowsky said. “I’m proud of them. In fact, it’s the violation of the first that’s given me pause over the past week.”

Mr. Malachowsky said that if the company adheres to those core values, it “will come out strong.” He urged employees to demonstrate those values in meetings and discussions.

“Keep these standards,” Mr. Malachowsky said. “Keep the culture alive. If we did our jobs well, and I think we did, we’re going to be fine.”

Ian Buck, the head of Nvidia’s data center business, said that the company didn’t need to worry about the road map it has developed for designing and manufacturing future generations of A.I. chips, which are the bedrock of the company’s business. He pointed to the leadership team beside him onstage and said, “We know how to get it done.”

Nvidia’s executive team said their business strategy won’t change. They plan to continue to support open models and close its acquisition of Hugging Face, a library of open A.I. models that Nvidia is purchasing for $12.9 billion. It is going to use those systems in its development of robotics and autonomous vehicles.

“All of that continues so we can become the leader of open models,” said Dwight Diercks, senior vice president of engineering.

Other executives made assurances about other key areas of the company’s business. They said Nvidia will maintain strong relationships with suppliers like Taiwan Manufacturing Semiconductor Company, which makes all its chips. They said the company would continue to outpace the industry in developing more powerful A.I. chips. And they will execute “a great business plan that endures.”

Nick Parker, who leads worldwide sales, said the company will expand its leadership ranks because it is “a great piece of the magic of how Nvidia delivers value.”

The leadership team had the benefit of the company’s latest earnings behind it. On Wednesday, the company reported quarterly profit and sales doubled, with revenue topping $100 billion for the first time. The results showed that the dominant maker of A.I. chips has momentum as the A.I. boom continues to expand.

The company said it will proceed with its Washington conference in December, which is scheduled the same week Mr. Huang and Tim Teter, the company’s general counsel, are expected to testify in a closed-door briefing with Congress. Mr. Huang is usually the ringmaster at those events. In his absence, other leaders at the company will share the stage for the keynote.

Ms. Kress, who joined the company 13 years ago, closed the nearly hourlong meeting by talking about her love of American football. Her son, who has been a student at the University of Florida, took her to a Gators football game. She marveled at the team’s third quarter tradition. when every fan in the stadium stands up and sings the team’s adopted anthem.

“It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony, singing that song,” she said. “You know what: We’re going to hear that song, and I believe in all of you that you’re going to help sing it.”

She sat back down as employees erupted in applause and the speakers filled with the guitar chords of Tom Petty’s “I Won’t Back Down.”

item.title: Jeff Bezos Says He Helped Pick Robert Pattinson as the New James Bond
item.description:
The Amazon founder Jeff Bezos said on Tuesday that he helped select Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond just days before the casting announcement this week.

Amazon acquired Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, the longtime home to the Bond franchise, in 2022 and has since gained creative control over future installments of the spy thriller series. The next film, starring Pattinson and directed by Denis Villeneuve, has no official release date but is expected to arrive in 2028 — closing what is on track to being the longest gap in the franchise’s history.

Bezos said he was “heavily involved” in the casting process, which had been shrouded in mystery. He was speaking at the Silicon Valley & The World conference hosted by the news outlet Semafor in Menlo Park, Calif.

He said the selection process began with a large group of candidates that was eventually whittled down to five finalists who recently performed screen tests in London. After final deliberations on Friday, Pattinson emerged as the top choice over Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner.

All five finalists were “extraordinarily talented,” Bezos said, “but there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.”

Initially, Bezos said, the selection group was hesitant about choosing Pattinson because he already had such a high profile.

“We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” Bezos said. The Bond franchise has typically cast actors who were not yet A-listers.

“But in the screening tests, it was so obvious,” Bezos said. “He is James Bond.”

Pattinson, the “Twilight” breakout who has had a blockbuster year with roles in Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” and Lance Oppenheim’s “Primetime,” will succeed Daniel Craig as the seventh actor to play 007 in the beloved series. Craig led five Bond films over 15 years, capping off his run in 2021 with “No Time to Die.”

“To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement,” Pattinson, 40, said in a statement to The New York Times.

Pattinson’s banner year is not over yet. Next month, he will appear in the star-studded final installment of Villeneuve’s “Dune” trilogy, joined by returning cast members Timothée Chalamet, Zendaya, Florence Pugh, Anya Taylor-Joy and Jason Momoa.

item.title: Fed Saw Need to Continue Raising Rates Despite October Skip
item.description:
Officials at the Federal Reserve broadly acknowledged the need to continue raising interest rates even as they voted against an increase at their October meeting, according to minutes from that gathering.

That record, released on Wednesday, indicated that for a few policymakers, October’s decisions was a “close call.” That reflected the heightened concern that many harbor about inflation, which has overshot the Fed’s 2 percent target for nearly six years. In recent months, price pressures have intensified more than expected even as the impact of President Trump’s tariffs have faded.

There was widespread recognition that the war with Iran and a surge in spending from artificial intelligence companies had made a broader range of goods and services more expensive.

“Several participants observed that tariff-related effects on prices appeared to be waning; however, most remarked that inflation pressures in the economy were broad based,” the minutes said. “The vast majority noted that high energy prices continued to contribute to current inflation pressures. Many participants observed that demand for products associated with the A.I. buildout was continuing to strain supply and raise prices of technology-related consumer goods, and several judged that price pressures were increasingly extending beyond industries directly affected by data center construction.”

The Fed’s decision to hold rates steady last month stemmed from a view adopted by several top policymakers that there was no urgency to rapidly lift borrowing costs after September’s quarter-point increase. That approach has been challenged in recent weeks as fresh consumer price data has affirmed that new sources of inflation appear to be cropping up across the economy.

Several officials have since embraced the need for swifter rate increases going forward, setting off an internal debate about just how fast to go. On Wednesday, Christopher J. Waller, a Fed governor, reiterated his view that the central bank should consider a half-point move when it next meets in December. In an interview with CNBC, he said it might be necessary to “shock people,” especially if the Fed did not explicitly signal that another rate increase in January was necessary.

John C. Williams, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, on Tuesday suggested that there was no need for “dramatic action,” even as he conceded that the central bank still had work to do on inflation. Instead, support seems to be coalescing around the idea of raising rates at consecutive meetings after a quarter-point increase next month. That would entail lifting borrowing costs again when the Fed meets at the end of January and then potentially doing so in mid-March if the data demanded it.

Some officials already supported a back-to-back cadence last month. Beth M. Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, and Lisa D. Cook, a central bank governor who is engaged in a protracted legal fight with President Trump over his efforts to oust her, dissented against a hold in favor of a quarter-point increase.

At a news conference after the rate decision, Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed chairman, stressed that the central bank had the flexibility to accrue more information about the state of the economy before taking additional steps to raise rates.

Mr. Warsh pointed to the fact that expectations about future inflation continued to show confidence in the Fed’s ability to return inflation to the 2 percent target. He also emphasized that credit conditions for households and businesses had become less favorable, which he said showed that “policy is working.”

U.S. stock markets have whipped around since the Fed last met. A.I. stocks have sold off sharply, first in the immediate wake of the midterm elections amid concerns that Democrats would usher in heightened regulatory scrutiny. More recently, they have buckled as a result of a shake-up at the chip maker Nvidia, whose chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned after revelations that he had two affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence services determined was feeding information to Beijing.

U.S. borrowing costs have also climbed since the central bank’s October gathering. The 10-year Treasury note, which serves as a global benchmark, now trades around 5 percent, while the yield on two-year Treasuries, which are sensitive to changes in the Fed’s rate expectations, have surged to around 4.8 percent.

item.title: Social Media Helped Build Hailey Bieber’s Company. It Also Took a Mental Toll.
item.description:
Hailey Bieber, the model and entrepreneur who sold her Rhode beauty brand for at least $800 million last year, said that even though she had relied on social media to build her company and her online persona, it was “distorting” and had challenged her mental health.

“It can be distorting to the mind, especially those filters that change your face — they make your lips bigger, your nose smaller,” Mrs. Bieber said. “That definitely can be harmful and misleading, 100 percent. But it’s part of the world we’re living in; it’s not going anywhere.”

The 29-year-old is emblematic of two recent booms: the rise of the social-media-star-turned-entrepreneur and the popularity of skin care products, which has sent girls as young as 11 flocking to Sephora for serums.

Mrs. Bieber, who is married to the pop star Justin Bieber and is a daughter of the actor Stephen Baldwin, co-founded Rhode with Lauren and Michael D. Ratner in 2022 and sold it to E.L.F. Beauty for $800 million in cash and stock last year, with a potential payout of $200 million based on sales targets over three years.

Rhode — which is Mrs. Bieber’s middle name — has surged as E.L.F. introduced its products, like $20 peptide lip tints and a $32 glazing milk, at Sephora. Celebrity-backed brands run the risk of being flashes in the pan, a concern analysts brought up when the deal was announced, but Rhode has thrived so far.

That’s partly because of Mrs. Bieber, who has nearly 60 million Instagram followers and almost 20 million on TikTok. She remains the brand’s chief creative officer and head of innovation, and many of her online posts are devoted to marketing Rhode. (Mr. Bieber has also fueled her brand, referencing Rhode’s popular iPhone case with a slot that holds a lip gloss in a song.)

Mrs. Bieber said that social media had made her feel insecure and depressed in the past.

“I had people telling me to kill myself in the comments every single day,” she said. “The way people were making me feel was that maybe it would be better if I wasn’t here anymore, because that’s how intense I felt other people’s feelings were toward me.”

She said that she viewed the best path forward as “open conversation about what that looks like and how it might make somebody feel.”

item.title: Tech Chiefs Express Empathy for Jensen Huang at DealBook Summit
item.description:
Jensen Huang, the former chief executive of chip giant Nvidia, wasn’t in the room at the DealBook Summit on Wednesday. But he was top of mind with some speakers.

Tech chiefs, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey, expressed empathy toward Mr. Huang following his resignation last week from Nvidia after reports of his affair with a woman that U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese asset.

“I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best. I don’t think the world needs another set of random opinions on what’s going to happen here,” Mr. Altman told Andrew Ross Sorkin.

Mr. Huang, seen as the face of artificial intelligence because of his company’s dominance in making the chips that power A.I., has received a groundswell of support in Silicon Valley. Start-ups are concerned that Mr. Huang’s exit could mean Nvidia, often called the “central bank of A.I.,” embraces a more conservative approach to investing and deal-making under its interim chief executive, Colette Kress.

Mr. Luckey posited a geopolitical angle. “China wants Jensen out, so I want him in,” the tech entrepreneur said.

Mr. Luckey differs with Mr. Huang in calling for tougher U.S. export controls on chips to China. He had tough words for reports about Mr. Huang’s affairs, but he insisted the man was irreplaceable.

“Jensen is the guy who built this company from scratch,” he said. “He deeply understands it. His personal relationships are the reasons that everyone is willing to do business.”

Mr. Altman has a more personal angle. He was ousted as chief executive in 2023 before being reinstated. That experience, he said, gave him more empathy toward Mr. Huang.

“One thing I did not appreciate was everybody on Earth speculating with some random theory here or there,” he said.

item.title: Anthropic’s Public Debut Sets Up ‘Experiment’ in Corporate Power
item.description:
Todd Underwood, a former Anthropic engineering leader, fielded a stream of calls in recent months from investment managers eager to gain his insider view on the artificial intelligence giant’s business strategy ahead of this week’s initial public offering.

But few of the questions focused on an aspect of the company Mr. Underwood viewed as a crucial asset: Anthropic’s unusual governance structure.

The company is set to become by far the most valuable company on the stock market with the legal designation of a public benefit corporation, or P.B.C. That status requires Anthropic to prioritize its corporate mission — to develop safe A.I. systems “for the long-term benefit of humanity” — in addition to the customary sole focus on value for stockholders.

The company’s public benefit mandate is guarded partly by a five-member “long-term benefit trust,” which includes Ben Bernanke, the former Federal Reserve chair.

The company “will choose to do things in favor of safety rather than in favor of making money,” said Mr. Underwood, who has been sought out by investors as a former employee for insights into the company. He added that he agreed with that focus but thought it might turn off some investors.

The company’s public offering sets up an important test as Anthropic goes from one of the most closely watched private companies in the world to one of the most scrutinized.

Anthropic is expected to spend its first two years as a publicly traded company asking investors for patience as it burns hundreds of billions of dollars of cash to invest in new chips and data centers. It is also facing increasing calls from A.I. safety advocates, as well as some of its own employees, to slow down its pace of training new models.

On Wednesday, the company is expected to sell roughly $65 billion in shares, making it the second-largest I.P.O. after SpaceX’s earlier this year. It also has $26 billion of investments lined up from tech giants like Nvidia and Microsoft.

Anthropic’s expected market capitalization, more than $1.4 trillion, would make it 30 times as valuable as the next public benefit corporation that trades on the stock market, the software maker Veeva Systems.

Anthropic was founded as a public benefit corporation in 2021, and formed its long-term benefit trust in 2023 as a way to give the structure teeth, ensuring the company balances goals for shareholders and its broader mission. The structure is taxed the same as any corporation.

The trust is made up of a group of “financially disinterested” experts in economics, science and global health who don’t own Anthropic stock, the company said in its offering prospectus. The group has the power to appoint and remove several of the company’s board members, authority that is typically given only to shareholders.

Adding to the unusual leadership structure, the company also spent the months leading up to its public offering locking in new authority for the executives who started the company nearly six years ago, according to securities filings.

The company created a new class of shares this fall for its unusually large co-founding team — seven executives, including the chief executive, Dario Amodei — that give them 50.1 percent of voting control over the company, collectively. The founders have the ability to appoint other board members.

A founder-controlled board committee can also help overrule one of the trust’s four board appointments, reducing the trust’s power, said Jesse M. Fried, a Harvard law professor who has studied Anthropic’s corporate structure.

The trust’s authority was “watered down” as a result of the changes, but they don’t “fundamentally change the governance of the company,” he added.

Anthropic’s structure is unique when compared with other publicly traded companies, corporate governance experts said.

“I don’t know if I can really compare it to anything else,” said Douglas Chia, a senior fellow at Rutgers Law School who advises companies on corporate governance. “It’s going to be an interesting experiment.”

The Council of Institutional Investors, an advocacy group that represents public, union and corporate pension funds, has long been critical of arrangements that give founders voting control disproportionate to their financial stakes. The group wrote a letter this year expressing concerns that when SpaceX went public, it gave its founder, Elon Musk, dominant voting control.

The group will “wait and see” how Anthropic’s structure plays out, said Glenn Davis, the council’s executive director. The founders’ immense voting power means that “ultimately the founders are accountable to themselves,” rather than shareholders, he added.

The layered structure could still challenge investors’ understanding of the company and the group of people who govern it, said Paul Abrahimzadeh, a senior partner at the tech investment firm 1979 Capital.

Still, investor enthusiasm was inevitable despite the uncertainties, he added. “You have to own it. The question is at what price?”

item.title: Palmer Luckey Warns the U.S. Faces an A.I. ‘Mismatch’
item.description:
Killer robots on the front lines of wars. Offshore structures where industry thrives without regulation. Palmer Luckey is trying to build a world that does not yet exist.

The home-schooled engineer and longtime supporter of President Trump’s is a founder of Anduril Industries, a defense tech company that builds artificial intelligence-powered drones valued at $61 billion. The famously opinionated founder spoke to Andrew Ross Sorkin on Wednesday at the DealBook Summit about A.I., his sometimes bellicose vision of the future and, for good measure, a decade-old grievance from his Facebook days.

Mr. Luckey, 34, started the discussion by addressing an issue that’s become top of mind: the widespread tech outages across the United States. He blamed attackers using A.I. tools to target outdated infrastructure. “There’s a mismatch between the attackers, who are very fast-moving in using technology and old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed,” he said.

“I think people are going to have to pick up the pace,” Mr. Luckey said about the need to patch up the country’s creaky digital infrastructure. “It’s time to start running.”

That could just as well describe Mr. Luckey’s position on innovation. He has argued that the best way to predict the future is to rush forward and build it, and he has had success with that philosophy.

While Anduril has collected just a tiny sliver of U.S. military spending, less than 1 percent, Mr. Luckey has captured the imagination of some top military brass. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth invited him to participate in Project Meridian, a 120-day strategic study to “map out the future of warfare.”

Mr. Luckey defended the endeavor on Wednesday, saying that there is a long tradition of the government brainstorming with members from the industry, despite concerns about potential conflicts of interest.

Mr. Luckey also discussed a new venture he’s backing, a “seastead” that will allow the industry to develop new businesses far from the long arm of regulators. He sees seasteading as ripe for commercialization that until now has been held back by engineering limitations.

Mr. Luckey sold the first company he co-founded, Oculus VR, to Facebook for about $2 billion in cash and stock in 2014. Although the sale allowed Mr. Luckey to later invest in seasteading and more, he has not forgiven Facebook for firing him, he said at the conference.

Mr. Luckey moved to Silicon Valley to join Facebook after it bought his company, but he clashed with his team over the direction of virtual reality. Before the 2016 presidential election, news that Mr. Luckey had donated $9,000 to a pro-Trump organization that erected a billboard insulting the Democratic nominee, Hillary Clinton, angered his Facebook, now Meta, colleagues. They demanded he be fired, he said, and he was in 2017.

Anduril Industries was his revenge project, he said. Based on the company’s rapid rise, revenge has been sweet.

But he hasn’t gotten over his firing nearly a decade ago. “I still take it very personally,” he said. “I have not let it go.”

item.title: Polymarket Founder Says Trump Jr.’s Involvement Is ‘Heavily Overblown’
item.description:
Shayne Coplan, the founder of Polymarket, defended his company’s partnership with Donald Trump Jr. on Wednesday, a week after a rival prediction market cut ties with the president’s oldest son.

The attention on the relationship is “heavily overblown,” Mr. Coplan said at the DealBook Summit in New York. “We have all types of investors.”

Mr. Trump has invested in Polymarket via 1789 Capital, his venture firm, raising concerns from critics who say the Trump stake creates a conflict of interest because the federal government regulates prediction markets.

Mr. Coplan said that most of his interactions with the president’s son were “fun conversations” about topics like hunting. “It’s fun to hear the stories,” he said. “It sounds like a really good time.”

At the summit, Mr. Coplan spoke onstage alongside Vlad Tenev, the chief executive of the trading app Robinhood, and Adena Friedman, the chair of the Nasdaq exchange. Much of the conversation centered on the blurry line between gambling and investment.

“I don’t want to be the one telling you that you can’t trade something,” Mr. Tenev said. “I shouldn’t be making that decision.”

Before this year, prediction markets like Polymarket occupied an obscure corner of the internet. Now they’re suddenly a cultural phenomenon, with people using the platforms to bet on everything from sports to the weather. Polymarket and its top rival, Kalshi, have each raised billions of dollars from investors and pushed expensive marketing campaigns, partnering with celebrities like LeBron James and Timothée Chalamet. Last month, Kalshi brought in $98 billion in trades, according to the Block, a data tracker.

Mr. Coplan became the early face of prediction markets in 2024, when Polymarket earned acclaim for successfully predicting Donald J. Trump’s victory in the presidential election. But lately, Polymarket has fallen behind Kalshi in the race for customers. It’s also facing courtroom battles with state attorneys general who argue that prediction markets are unlicensed gambling operations without the proper regulations.

After Mr. Trump was elected, Polymarket and Kalshi each forged ties with the president’s oldest son. Donald Trump Jr. served as an adviser to Kalshi and received shares in the company. He also advised Polymarket and invested alongside his partners at 1789 Capital.

Kalshi said last week that Donald Trump Jr. would no longer serve as an adviser, citing his firm’s investment in Polymarket. A spokesman for the president’s son confirmed that the decision was mutual.

item.title: Microsoft’s Chief Warns That A.I. Makes More Outages Likely
item.description:
Less than a week after Microsoft’s global Outlook outage, Satya Nadella, the company’s chief executive, warned that a prolonged period of “instability” for global infrastructure might be coming.

In comments at the DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday, Mr. Nadella said that A.I. tools were finding cybersecurity bugs at a breakneck pace, and that companies were having to create fixes and deploy them “instantaneously” because the bugs were actively “being exploited in the wild.” That kind of speed gives companies less time to test the patches as in the past, he said, and could lead to more buggy updates being pushed into operation.

Mr. Nadella said Microsoft’s outage was the result of a “perfect storm” of events that set off a “latent bug” in its infrastructure. Last week’s problem knocked millions of people, along with businesses and governments, around the globe off their email for about a day

The company said the outage was rooted in a software update Microsoft made over the summer that was tested on older equipment. The issue only became apparent, it said, when more traffic, resulting from two other problems, was pushed onto the servers. At its worst, more than 80 percent of Microsoft’s servers were unresponsive.

Mr. Nadella said that with A.I. efficiently discovering new vulnerabilities, online systems can have “essentially a nation-state level persistent attacker going after you all the time, so that means we have a lot of fragility.” The problem becomes more difficult with physical infrastructure, like transportation and heating and cooling systems, he said, that are connected to the internet but harder to update.

Mr. Nadella said he was unsure when — or whether — the situation would improve. He pointed to the late 1990s, when the world fretted about whether a quirk in common computer code would cause a global meltdown when the year 2000 arrived. But “Y2K was one bug, and one day,” Mr. Nadella said. A.I. systems, however, have continued to improve, and he is not yet sure how the race between hackers and defenders will balance out.

item.title: Mamdani Talks Trump, Taxes and Oct. 7 at DealBook Summit
item.description:
Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, acknowledged the elephant in the room on Wednesday afternoon. Mr. Mamdani, a democratic socialist, was speaking at a conference marketed to, and attended by, the very business leaders who so often look askance at his rhetoric and economic theory.

“Comrades,” he said, flashing a smile and eliciting chuckles from the crowd at the DealBook Summit, “it’s great to be here at the largest D.S.A. meeting Lincoln Center has ever seen.” He was referring to the Democratic Socialists of America.

What followed was a wide-ranging 30-minute discussion on everything from the midterm elections and his remarkably amicable relationship with President Trump to his approach to antisemitism. Mr. Mamdani, who has become known among reporters for his message discipline, rarely deviated from his standard rhetoric.

Mr. Mamdani came up in the pro-Palestinian movement, founding a chapter of Students for Justice in Palestine at Bowdoin College and sponsoring legislation in the Assembly that would strip tax-exempt status from nonprofits with ties to Israeli settler groups. His support for Palestinians and critique of Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state remain core to his beliefs.

But those beliefs do not necessarily endear him to a crowd of business leaders, many of them more moderate than him, many of them Jewish, many of them at Lincoln Center on Wednesday afternoon.

Pressed on antisemitism and complaints from some Jewish New Yorkers that his statement on Oct. 7, the anniversary of attacks on Israel, paid too little attention to the Israeli victims and too much to the Palestinian victims that followed, Mr. Mamdani argued that the two were inherently connected.

“When the Israeli government is conducting a genocide of Palestinians, oftentimes the defense that will be given, no matter what day that it’s asked about, will be the relationship to Oct. 7,” he said. “My point being, this is a day that is not only a horrific war crime, it is also a day that has been used as a justification for all that followed it. And it is in that day that it is important, like in any day, to mourn the totality of its impact.”

He was also asked about Ken Griffin, the hedge fund C.E.O. with whom he feuded this year.

In April, Mr. Mamdani filmed a video in front of Mr. Griffin’s multistory midtown penthouse discussing the decision by Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York to pursue a new tax on high-end second homes in New York City.

“Today, we’re taxing the rich,” he said, naming Mr. Griffin and pointing to the apartment that the chief executive bought for $238 million, which he cast as Exhibit A in why the tax was necessary. The video has been viewed more than 53 million times on X.

Mr. Griffin responded with fury, describing the video as “creepy and weird” and suggesting that Mr. Mamdani had put a target on his back.

Mr. Mamdani “seems to have forgotten that the C.E.O. of another American company was assassinated just blocks from where I live in New York,” he said, referring to the 2024 murder of Brian Thompson, the UnitedHealthcare chief executive.

Mr. Griffin even issued an ultimately empty threat to pull out of a deal to build a new office tower on Park Avenue. Steven Roth, the Vornado Realty Trust chief executive with whom Mr. Griffin is building that tower, likened Mr. Mamdani’s remarks to hate speech.

On Wednesday, Mr. Mamdani declined to say whether, given the backlash, he would make that video again.

“You know, you never make the same video twice,” he said. “That’s the video that we made.”

item.title: How Nvidia Chips Ended Up Within Reach of China’s Military
item.description:
In 2023, as the artificial intelligence boom took off, Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were pitching investors in Shanghai on a plan to build an A.I. business in Southeast Asia.

Working from a colonial mansion in the city’s former French Concession neighborhood, the couple boasted about Ms. Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang, then Nvidia’s chief executive, who they said would guarantee a supply of powerful computer chips.

They also hinted at a deep-pocketed customer that would pay for access to those chips and anchor the business, according to two people who attended the meetings. The company created after those pitch sessions, a Singapore firm called Megaspeed, purchased more than $4 billion in Nvidia chips over the next few years.

Megaspeed’s customer and financial backer turned out to be Alibaba, the Chinese internet giant, according to three people familiar with the relationship. Alibaba is a colossus, with a wide range of businesses. It also co-founded an A.I. lab with strong ties to China’s military, where researchers have worked on tasks such as automating cyberattacks and simulating war games.

For the past several weeks, Nvidia has been convulsed by revelations that Mr. Huang had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials say is an asset for Chinese intelligence and was passing information to Beijing. But beneath the scandal is a geopolitical tug of war over access to the advanced Nvidia chips that help power the global A.I. boom.

The web of relationships between Megaspeed, Alibaba and Nvidia exposes a supply chain that often circumvents efforts by the United States to keep those chips out of China’s reach. The fact that Alibaba has access to the Nvidia chips and is only one step removed from the military-linked A.I. lab is exactly what intelligence officials in Washington have long feared. The technology could help China develop more sophisticated weapons, carry out cyberattacks and integrate A.I. into the battlefield.

The facility, called Zhejiang Lab, has another important link to Nvidia. Its current director, Wang Jian, was Alibaba’s chief technology officer and has had a long friendship with Nvidia’s Mr. Huang.

Whether Nvidia chips supplied by Megaspeed went from Alibaba to the lab is unclear. But the ties show how advanced computing reaches sensitive Chinese institutions through layers of contractors and resellers that obscure the origin of the chips. It also underscores how closely Alibaba, the company that anchored Ms. Huang’s business, was bound to the Chinese state.

The lab’s ties to Megaspeed and Ms. Huang’s business network, which ran through Alibaba and another smaller company, have not been previously reported, and raise the possibility that Megaspeed is providing Nvidia chips to support research for China’s military, which would violate U.S. law.

Megaspeed would buy chips for an offshore data center. Alibaba was its biggest customer. Together, the arrangement let Alibaba tap the powerful A.I. chips that American rules were meant to bar from China.

The complex ties, some of which were formed over the course of Mr. Huang’s roughly two decades doing business in China, raise questions about the checks Nvidia was supposed to conduct of its customers. The chips flowed to one of China’s largest tech companies at a moment when the Chinese leader Xi Jinping was pulling such companies closer into the orbit of the security state.

In 2022, Nvidia’s sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the relationship. The introduction was first reported by The Information.

In Washington, the Nvidia scandal has inflamed an ongoing debate over access to powerful A.I. chips, as the fallout grows for the chip-making giant. Mr. Huang resigned last week after revelations that he also had another affair with an employee, and the U.S. government is investigating whether Megaspeed smuggled chips into China.

Mr. Huang has regularly dismissed the possibility that China’s military was interested in his product. He has argued that the Chinese military would never rely on American chips because Washington could block their export at any time, even as China’s military issued hundreds of public tenders seeking them. Mr. Huang did not respond to an emailed request for comment.

“Nvidia works across the industry to comply with the evolving rules regarding cloud services, while competing to build American infrastructure in every approved region,” said John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia.

James Tan, the chief executive of Megaspeed, declined to comment on the connections between Alibaba, Megaspeed and military-linked institutions, saying in an emailed response that “this matter remains under independent review and that the company has not reached any conclusions.” Compliance with U.S. law is extremely important to Megaspeed, he said.

Evidence linking Chinese companies like Alibaba to the government and military often hides in plain sight, in academic journals, public procurement documents, government statements and patent filings. The New York Times also analyzed hundreds of Chinese records and interviewed a dozen people close to the process.

“Any suggestions that Alibaba provides services to the military is groundless. Alibaba Cloud’s service agreement strictly prohibits the use of our products and services for any military purpose,” an Alibaba spokeswoman wrote in a statement. In June, the company sued the U.S. government after the Pentagon put it on a list of companies it said are contributing to China’s military. The case is ongoing.

A spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in the United States said “the ‘Chinese spy’ allegation is purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China. China opposes politicizing and instrumentalizing trade and tech issues.”

Zhejiang Lab did not respond to emailed questions.

During a visit to Beijing in 2025, Mr. Huang spoke at an event with one of China’s most revered technologists, Wang Jian.

Mr. Wang created Alibaba’s cloud unit and pioneered some of its biggest A.I. projects. In more recent years, he had also been pulled deeper into China’s security state. By the time the two met onstage, Mr. Wang was the director of the military-linked Zhejiang Lab.

“He is the hero. He’s an incredible hero. A superhero,” Mr. Huang said to Mr. Wang onstage, noting his work with young people. It is not clear if he knew of the lab’s military ties.

Mr. Huang’s relationship with Mr. Wang stretched back more than a decade. After Mr. Wang built Alibaba’s cloud unit, it became one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, buying chips for a cloud service that was used by businesses and government.

The warmth between the two was reminiscent of an era when U.S.-Chinese relations were far better and China’s leaps in technology were viewed positively in Washington and Silicon Valley.

But over the duration of Mr. Huang’s long friendship with Mr. Wang, relations between their two countries darkened as Mr. Xi drew private technology companies into the sphere of state security.

Things changed for Mr. Huang, too. He had become a tech industry kingmaker, and his chips a strategic asset for governments. The U.S. government had begun restricting the sale of some Nvidia chips to China.

At the end of the 2025 meeting, Mr. Huang called Mr. Wang a “good friend,” and put an arm around him as they walked off the stage.

A few weeks before, Mr. Wang had taken a role even closer to the military as an expert adviser to the People’s Liberation Army’s National University of Defense Technology, according to a public announcement not widely reported. The institute was placed on a United States trade blacklist in 2015 over supercomputers that were believed to use American chips to simulate nuclear explosions.

Co-founded by Alibaba in 2017, Zhejiang Lab is the epitome of recent Chinese government efforts to blend civilian and military science. Some of its researchers probe the origin of radio bursts from distant galaxies. Others partner with counterparts in the Chinese military. One area of focus was combining A.I. with hacking techniques, according to a job posting. Other topics of research included remote sensing, automated cyberdefense and vulnerability identification, and information campaigns.

A postdoctoral researcher who listed the lab as her affiliation co-wrote a paper with scientists at a Chinese air force academy that described how to use computer simulations to war-game how to destroy or force away a foreign aircraft carrier group that had come to support an island’s bid for independence.

Some of the work done by researchers at the lab has run on Nvidia chips, which are more powerful and more popular than those of Chinese rivals. Nvidia researchers even copublished studies with authors from Zhejiang Lab.

Alibaba also won contracts for three stages of a computing center that provincial officials describe as built by the lab. The contracts were issued by a state-owned company, Zhejiang Computility, that sells computing power to the lab. Zhejiang Computility advertises access to export-controlled Nvidia chips. The technical specifications in a separate contract it signed with another supplier match those of Nvidia chips.

Mr. Wang has said insufficient access to A.I. computing power has held China back.

“If China is to walk at the forefront of artificial intelligence,” he said, “we still lack high-quality computing power.”

But when Zhejiang Computility sought bids for the computing cluster in 2024, Nvidia was barred from selling chips that powerful to China. Another supplier to the company that year, Hangjin Technology, has a joint venture with Century Litong, another company linked to Mr. Kang and Ms. Huang, the former Megaspeed executive.

In September 2025, a few months after Mr. Huang’s visit with Mr. Wang, Nvidia and Alibaba announced a new collaboration: Nvidia’s robotic development tools would be integrated into Alibaba’s cloud to help train autonomous vehicles and robots.

In December 2023, Jensen Huang’s company plane made an overnight stop in Malaysia during a tour of Asia to meet with the country’s prime minister, Anwar Ibrahim. Announcing a deal for a data center in the country’s southern state of Johor, Mr. Huang said Malaysia had the potential to become an A.I. “manufacturing” hub for the world.

The project, on a former palm plantation larger than Central Park, was to be built by the Malaysian industrial conglomerate YTL. Nvidia pledged to provide some of its most advanced chips.

The setup was part of a multibillion-dollar data center boom underway in Malaysia that has made it one of the world’s largest computing hubs. Across the southern state of Johor, cranes swirl over massive construction projects underway to meet the demand from Chinese and American companies.

It is here that these webs of companies from China, Singapore and elsewhere form the opaque supply chains.

At the YTL facility, Megaspeed’s subsidiary, Speedmatrix, operated Nvidia chips inside the facility on behalf of Alibaba, according to five people familiar with the project who were not authorized to speak publicly.

Computer systems running on YTL’s network at the facility also bear Alibaba’s name, according to an infrastructure analysis by InfraWatch, an intelligence firm. That included software to remotely monitor equipment at a data center.

YTL did not respond to requests for comment.

The arrangement shows how Alibaba used a network of companies in Malaysia and other Southeast Asian countries to access powerful Nvidia chips that they would not otherwise be able to purchase or bring to China.

Alibaba’s links to the YTL facility in Malaysia help explain how the process worked, according to two people familiar with the development.

First, Alibaba would pledge to be a customer of a regional company, like Megaspeed. Then Megaspeed would use that agreement to raise money from investors to buy Nvidia chips, said the people. After securing the chips, Megaspeed struck more deals with companies like YTL that built data centers to operate the chips. Sometimes, the people said, chips bound for the data center were smuggled into China.

Once the facilities were up and running in recent years, Alibaba and its customers could access the Nvidia chips remotely. From the Malaysian data center, fiber optic cables send data to an internet connection hub in Singapore, which then links to China through undersea cables.

American officials believe China’s military uses the overseas data centers to train A.I. models, but then runs its A.I. operations from facilities inside China.

Nvidia’s Mr. Huang argued that China’s government would never accept the security risks of using foreign data centers and chips. But China-linked companies are involved at each step of the process.

Megaspeed buys its Nvidia servers from a company called Aivres, which is an American subsidiary of Inspur, a Chinese tech giant with deep state ties. At Megaspeed's new data center, repairs and installation are also done by engineers from another Shanghai company, connected to Ms. Huang, according to two people familiar with the operations.

Other Chinese tech giants have created similar arrangements to access Nvidia chips. In Southeast Asia, data center companies including DayOne, Bridge Data Centers and Aolani provide computing power to customers based in China, according to public records and people familiar with the deals.

DayOne and Bridge Data Centers did not respond to requests for comment. Aolani declined to comment about its customers.

Now the future of the boom has been thrown into question. American officials recently strengthened export rules to prevent companies like Alibaba from remotely accessing Nvidia’s chips.

That puts projects like the YTL facility in Malaysia in the spotlight. YTL’s stock price fell about 20 percent over two weeks as scrutiny grew of Megaspeed’s operations in the country.

If things go bad for Megaspeed, Alibaba put a contingency in place. A business agreement between an Alibaba subsidiary and Megaspeed pledges all servers, chips, intellectual property, and other equipment back to Alibaba if Megaspeed fails to meet its contractual obligations.

Ana Swanson contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: ‘I’m Not MAGA’: Musk Plays Down G.O.P. Support After Midterm Loss
item.description:
In the run-up to the midterm elections, Elon Musk deployed both his wealth — to the tune of nearly $500 million — and his public influence to help Republican candidates win.

But in the wake of Democrats’ resounding victory at the ballot box, Mr. Musk is seeking to portray himself as more of a political moderate, saying, “There are positives and negatives in both parties.”

“I’m not MAGA,” Mr. Musk, the chief executive of SpaceX and Tesla, said at the DealBook Summit on Wednesday. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”

(Mr. Musk has previously declared himself MAGA — and even “dark gothic MAGA.”)

Mr. Musk’s remarks were his most extensive to date after his midterms spending spree flopped. He bluntly said his effort “failed, by the way, obviously.” And it had him questioning, at an existential level, whether spending money on politics even worked.

Mr. Musk spent more money on the election than any person ever has in a cycle where they themselves were not the candidate.

What about his spending millions in support of losing candidates like Ken Paxton, who ran for the Senate in Texas? “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Mr. Musk conceded. “Probably if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”

The pivot by Mr. Musk was the latest effort by business leaders to grapple with the aftermath of the midterms, particularly as newly empowered Democrats took aim at billionaires and businesses like data centers.

Throughout the interview, Mr. Musk largely avoided the often fiery (and sometimes profane) declarations that punctuated his last appearance at the DealBook Summit, in 2023. He predicted that things in Texas would be “fine” under Gina Hinojosa, the incoming Democratic governor, who supports maintaining a moratorium on new data centers in the state. Mr. Musk, a Texas resident, called her “quite moderate” and “not a far-left governor.”

Mr. Musk spoke at length about less politically divisive topics, like potentially merging SpaceX and Tesla and helping humanity achieve interstellar travel.

He also defended Jensen Huang, the former chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, whom he described as “a friend of mine” and whom he supported returning to that role. Though American intelligence considers that an executive whom Mr. Huang had an affair with was a Chinese intelligence asset, Mr. Musk said, “I don’t think he’s disloyal to the United States.”

Still, Mr. Musk was willing to be combative, particularly when it came to Ukraine.

Addressing restrictions on the Ukrainian military’s access to the satellite communications network that SpaceX runs, Mr. Musk said that the system, Starlink, was never meant to be used for offensive strikes in war.

“Do not ask me as a private individual to make kill decisions that sometimes result in the loss of innocent lives,” Mr. Musk said.

When asked about claims by Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, that his country’s forces were using the military version of Starlink — which can be used for attacks — Mr. Musk shot back, “He’s not always truthful.”

item.title: 6 Takeaways From the 2026 DealBook Summit
item.description:
The promise and peril of artificial intelligence, America’s shifting politics and what it means for businesses and global trade, the reverberations of Jensen Huang’s ouster at Nvidia on Silicon Valley and Wall Street, and more dominated the discussions at the annual DealBook Summit on Wednesday.

Over the course of the day, speakers, including Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, dug into A.I.’s growth (and security) challenges. There was also plenty of chatter about the speakers’ relationships with President Trump before and since Election Day, including from Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York.

There were quirkier moments, too. Polymarket’s chief executive, Shayne Coplan, said he had A.I. agents trading on his laptop in his green room as he spoke.

The annual summit, hosted by Andrew Ross Sorkin, founder of DealBook, has taken place since 2011.

Here are six main themes that emerged.

The morning started off with comments on the debate that has gripped Wall Street: Is the recent tech-stock sell-off a blip, or a sign the A.I. industry is doomed to run out of steam? Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, warned that while growth in A.I. had helped keep the global economy resilient, it might not end well. There is a “very ambitious price valuation which stands to be corrected eventually,” she said.

On the flip side, Mr. Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, an A.I. powerhouse expected to go public as soon as next year, downplayed the “ups and downs of valuations.” Overall, he said, the “trend is going to be strong.”

The debate took on extra emphasis with Anthropic pricing a record-setting I.P.O. valuing the giant at more than $1.5 trillion. Its shares are set to begin trading on Thursday.

“These companies are remarkably consequential companies for the future of the economy, the future of society,” said Adena Friedman, chief executive of Nasdaq, whose stock exchange will list Anthropic’s shares.

Beyond the financial fears of how fast the A.I. industry is growing is a fear of how powerful the technology itself has become. Greg Brockman, a founder at OpenAI and its president, said A.I. safety had become a bigger conversation (and focus at his company) as models became more capable.

“Models are now capable enough that we need to think about safety, security, alignment — that’s new,” he said. “And that’s actually been a huge cultural shift.”

Both he and Mr. Altman stressed the need for humans to retain a tight control of the technology. Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, for one, sounded skeptical that so-called alignment — the science of teaching A.I. to broadly follow human preferences and instructions — is fully possible.

Palmer Luckey, chief executive of defense behemoth Anduril, sees a potential dark cloud, however. He said he believe the recent wave of tech outages bedeviling airlines, banks and our digital lives had an A.I. angle. He blamed attackers using A.I. tools to target outdated infrastructure.

“As of right now, there’s a mismatch between the attackers, who are very fast-moving in using technology and old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed,” he said.

Mayor Mamdani of New York City explained a bit about how he maintains an amicable relationship with President Trump. Mr. Mamdani, a democratic socialist, said the key to dealing with the president was “to focus on any possible area of commonality — and the reason for that is the stakes are so immense.”

He gave the example of how he called the president to plead his case, asking for a relaxation of rules to help the city’s bodegas and small retailers meet new federal food-stocking rules

Prime Minister Carney of Canada who met with Mr. Trump earlier in the day on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, has found negotiations on the countries’ trade spat progressing slower than he’d like.

But he also offered a paradoxical view. In certain settings, Mr. Trump comes across as personable and engaged.

“He listens a lot more in private,” Mr. Carney said. “I mean, he’s interested, genuinely, in your opinion, and it’s a reasonably direct conversation.” Even so, Canada is advancing trade ties with China while talks with the Trump administration remain stalled over their tit-for-tat tariff war.

Governance watchdogs have long called into question business figures’ close ties to the president and his family — an issue that could draw serious scrutiny from a Democrat-controlled congress.

David Ellison, chief executive of Skydance, could be one under the political microscope. In conversation with Mr. Sorkin, Mr. Ellison took on issues as big as press freedom and as small as Rush Hour 4. Skydance’s decision to greenlight production of the film was for creative and commercial reasons, Mr. Ellison said, not because the studio was pressured to do so by Mr. Trump, who was previously reported to have requested the studio to revive the franchise.

Mr. Ellison’s media conglomerate, Paramount Skydance, was born out of a mega merger with Warner Bros. after the Justice Department this summer shuttered its investigation into the deal. Mr. Ellison’s father, Larry Ellison, has a close relationship with Mr. Trump.

“We’ve been fortunate enough to be able to work closely with this administration,” Mr. Ellison said. But, he added, “when we started the Paramount deal, that was under the Biden administration” with whom “we were working very closely.”

Later in the day, Mr. Coplan of Polymarket defended his company’s ties to Donald Trump Jr., the president’s oldest son, who’s an investor in the company via his venture firm 1789 Capital, saying the relationship is “heavily overblown.”

The tech bosses on the agenda — Mr. Altman, Mr. Luckey of Anduril and Mr. Nadella of Microsoft — all expressed empathy toward Mr. Huang’s predicament after his ouster last week from Nvidia after reports of his affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese asset.

Some in the Trump administration have suggested Nvidia’s parting with Mr. Huang, who has said he would like a shot to return to the chip making giant, is the right move. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week that the company needed a “dramatic shake-up” — widely interpreted as a call for new blood to run Nvidia.

Tech leaders have had kinder words. Mr. Altman told Andrew Ross Sorkin: “I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best. I don’t think the world needs another set of random opinions on what’s going to happen here.”

Mr. Musk, like others in Silicon Valley, said Mr. Huang was irreplaceable.

“Let’s say you’re the Chicago Bulls, middle of your second season, and you’ve got a winning streak that’s just going to happen, and then you kick Michael Jordan off your team,” Mr. Musk said, adding that “doesn’t seem like a smart decision to me.”

Prediction markets, platforms that allow users to wager on real-world events like election outcomes and sports, have taken financial markets by storm.

Traders on Polymarket, for example, can and have wagered on what speakers at the DealBook Summit would say. Such bets have drawn heavy scrutiny.

“Mention markets are entertaining, that’s for sure,” said Vlad Tenev, chief executive of Robinhood, whose company has banned such wagers. “But they’re also easy to manipulate.”

Mr. Coplan of Polymarket had a more charitable view about the rise of prediction markets in general, arguing it is giving rise to a new type of savvy investor.

“People have gravitated to that as an information source,” he said. “And that’s the thing that I’m really excited about.”

Some speakers also talked about being way too online.

Hailey Bieber, the entrepreneur who sold her Rhode beauty brand for at least $800 million last year, said she was “100 percent” a social media addict. She, too, feels insecure after looking at people online, she said.

“It can be distorting to the mind, especially those filters that change your face. They make your lips bigger, your nose smaller,” she says. “That definitely can be harmful and misleading.”

item.title: Have High Gas Prices Made You Change How You Drive? Tell Us About It.
item.description:
Life has become a lot more expensive this year, in no small part because the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has caused prices at the pump to soar.

We want to hear how you’re coping. Are you driving less or cutting spending elsewhere to make sure you can afford fuel? Did you decide it was time to buy an electric or hybrid vehicle?

Your input will help us cover the fallout from the 2026 oil shock, as we try to understand how this crisis may reshape energy use in the long run.

If we have follow-up questions or are interested in including your experience in an upcoming article, we’ll reach out. We won’t publish your response without first letting you know.
